passage: Dear Diary, Our relay team practised again today. Miss put me with Samir, the new boy who sits at the back. Dadi always says we shouldn't mix with families of other faiths, so at first I didn't pass him the baton properly. I dropped it twice. Then Samir said, "Hold it lower, like this," and showed me. His hands were covered in the same chalk dust as mine. At break we shared my aloo paratha and his dates. He supports the same football team as Chachu! He's scared of Mrs Kapoor's maths tests, just like me. I don't know what's so different. Tomorrow I'll ask Dadi what she meant. We won the practice race. - Minakshi

passage: When the school kabaddi team needed one more raider, Sir picked Kiran, whose family had come from a state far to the east to work at the brick kiln. Baljeet, eleven and team captain, frowned. At the tea shop he'd heard the men say kiln families were "not like us" and couldn't be trusted. For a week he barely spoke to Kiran. Then, in the match against the next village, Kiran's quick raid saved Baljeet from being tagged out. Afterwards they sat on the canal wall, sharing a bottle of water. Kiran talked about missing a grandmother back home. Baljeet talked about missing his older brother, who worked in the city. "That's the same thing," Kiran said. Baljeet nodded. It was.

qa.q: Where had Kiran's family come to work?
qa.a: At the brick kiln.

qa.q: What did Baljeet realise on the canal wall?
qa.a: He realised that Kiran missing a grandmother and his own missing his brother were the same feeling, so the differences he had been told about felt small.

qa.q: What was the turning point in Baljeet's view of Kiran?
qa.a: Kiran's quick raid saved Baljeet in the match, which led to sitting together and talking honestly.

qa.q: What might that first week have been like for Kiran?
qa.a: Kiran, new and barely spoken to by the captain, probably felt shut out and unsure of being welcome on the team.

grounding: A village boy who had absorbed distrust of a migrant family befriends a teammate from another region through kabaddi and finds the differences small.

passage: Marek, ten, had heard his older cousin say that the new families from South America at the edge of Krakow were loud and rough. So when Ms Nowak paired him with Santiago for the spaghetti-bridge project, Marek groaned inside. The first afternoon they barely spoke. On the second, their bridge collapsed, and Santiago laughed so hard that Marek laughed too. Santiago was good at triangles. Marek was good at glue. By Friday their bridge held three dictionaries, the most in the class. Walking out, Santiago invited Marek to his cousin's birthday. Marek thought about his own cousin's words and couldn't match them to the boy beside him, who liked the same comics and hated beetroot too.

qa.q: How many dictionaries did their bridge hold?
qa.a: Three dictionaries, the most in the class.

qa.q: What was Marek feeling when Ms Nowak paired him with Santiago?
qa.a: He groaned inside, uneasy because of what his cousin had said about the new families.

qa.q: What in the project helped Marek let go of his cousin's words?
qa.a: Working together on the bridge, laughing when it fell and using each other's skills, gave him real knowledge of Santiago to set against the rumour.

qa.q: How might Santiago have seen that first quiet afternoon?
qa.a: Santiago may have noticed Marek's distance and felt unsure, yet still laughed and later invited Marek to a birthday.

grounding: A boy who learned wariness of newcomers from his cousin works on a class project with a boy from another region and finds the imagined differences small.

In the school library, the Class 5 water-cycle project paired Sumit with Sabina. Sumit's older cousin had once told him to keep away from families like hers, as if they were a different kind of people, so he sat at the far edge of the table.
But the model needed four hands: one to hold the plastic sheet over the bowl, one to tape it, two to pour the warm water. By the second afternoon they were arguing about whether clouds are wet, and laughing when the tape stuck in Sumit's hair.
On Thursday Sabina said her nani told ghost stories in every power cut. "Mine too!" Sumit said. "Does yours have a headless postman?" It did.
When the model won second prize, Sumit carried it and Sabina carried the ribbon. On the bus home he couldn't remember what his cousin had meant.

qa.q: What project were Sumit and Sabina paired on?
qa.a: The Class 5 water-cycle project.

qa.q: Why did Sumit sit at the far edge of the table at first?
qa.a: He had absorbed his cousin's warning about families like Sabina's and felt wary of her before knowing her.

qa.q: What turned the wariness into friendship?
qa.a: Needing four hands made them work together, and finding shared things like the ghost stories showed the differences were small.

qa.q: What might Sabina have noticed when Sumit sat at the far edge?
qa.a: She may have felt unwelcome or puzzled, which makes the later laughter and the shared ribbon mean even more.

grounding: A boy wary of a classmate from another faith because of a cousin's words finds the differences small while working with her on a shared project.

passage:
I'm Salma, Nazia's older sister, and I watched this whole thing from our balcony in the new Hyderabad colony. When a Tamil-speaking family moved into B-block, some aunties said they were "different" and their children "rough". Nazia, nine, repeated it at dinner.
Then the colony cricket team got a new player: Gowri, from B-block, who bowled faster than any boy. Nazia kept wicket for her. I can't tell you what went on in my sister's head, but I saw them practise every evening, counting runs in two languages and swapping words. Last week Nazia came home with a steel box of lemon rice from Gowri's mother and ate every grain.
At dinner someone repeated the "rough" line. Nazia put her spoon down. "Gowri isn't rough. She just bowls fast."

qa.q: What did Nazia bring home from Gowri's mother?
qa.a: A steel box of lemon rice.

qa.q: What might Nazia putting her spoon down at dinner suggest about her feelings?
qa.a: It suggests she now feels protective of Gowri and no longer believes the fear she once repeated.

qa.q: What helped Nazia's view change?
qa.a: Playing on the same cricket team, keeping wicket for Gowri and practising together every evening, so knowing Gowri replaced the aunties' words.

qa.q: How might Gowri have felt about the colony before joining the team?
qa.a: Gowri may have felt unwelcome and watched, which is why having Nazia as a teammate and friend could matter a lot.

grounding: An older sister watches a nine-year-old befriend a girl from another region through the colony cricket team and drop the fear she had picked up from adults.

passage: Vishal, you ask why Farzana-nani comes for every Diwali even though she's Muslim? Sit, I'll tell you. When I was ten, in Lucknow, our kho-kho team needed one more girl. Coach picked Farzana, from the lane behind the mosque. My chachi had always said, "Don't eat at their houses." I didn't even know why. For the first week I didn't talk to her. Then in our match against Christ Church school, Farzana and I had to chase together. She tagged three girls in one run. We screamed and hugged. Afterwards she shared her tiffin: aloo paratha, same as mine. Hers had more achar. That was all. After that we walked home together every day, and her Ammi made me sewaiyan at Eid. The big difference everyone warned me about? It fit in a tiffin box. So, Aparna-nani's oldest friend is Farzana. Now go eat your laddoo.

qa.q: What did Farzana share after the match?
qa.a: Farzana shared her tiffin: aloo paratha.

qa.q: What was Aparna feeling in the first week with Farzana on the team?
qa.a: Aparna felt wary and distant, carrying chachi's warning without knowing why, so she didn't talk to Farzana.

qa.q: Why was the match against Christ Church a turning point in the story?
qa.a: Having to chase together gave them a shared goal and a joyful win, which let Aparna see Farzana as a person instead of a warning.

qa.q: How might Farzana have felt in that first week when Aparna ignored her?
qa.a: Farzana may have felt left out and lonely on a new team, which makes the later hug and walks home more meaningful.

passage: The science-fair project was due at nine the next morning, and the power had gone out across the Ludhiana colony. Jasleen, eleven, and Arnab, new from Kolkata, crouched over a water-filter model by candlelight on her verandah. Jasleen's cousins had teased her about her partner: "Bengalis only eat fish and argue." She'd been wary for the first few days. But Arnab had fixed their leaking bottle with a hairclip, shared his mother's sandesh, and laughed at exactly the same cartoon she liked. Now he was carefully cutting charcoal layers while she held the torch. "Your turn," he said, handing her the scissors. "You're neater." By midnight the filter dripped clean water. They grinned at each other, soot on their faces. Jasleen realised she'd stopped noticing he was from anywhere.

qa.q: What did Arnab use to fix the leaking bottle?
qa.a: Arnab fixed their leaking bottle with a hairclip.

qa.q: What was Jasleen feeling about Arnab by midnight?
qa.a: Jasleen felt warm and at ease with Arnab, her early wariness replaced by friendship built on their shared work.

qa.q: What helped Jasleen move past her cousins' teasing?
qa.a: Working closely with Arnab on the project, and seeing him as a real person who shares her jokes and helps, chipped away at the learned stereotype.

qa.q: How might Arnab have felt being new in the colony?
qa.a: Arnab may have felt like an outsider at first, so being trusted as an equal partner likely helped him feel welcome.

passage: Tanvir, ten, had never been to Madhuri's house. His Dadi said families like hers "keep to themselves" and he should too. But when they both made the Pune under-11 cricket squad, the coach put them in the same practice pair. For two weeks they barely spoke, just nodded between balls. Then one evening Madhuri's bowling went wild and she almost cried. Tanvir walked over. "Your wrist is bending. Try it like this." She tried. The ball went straight. After practice she offered him her water bottle. They found out they both hated karela, both liked spy stories and both had a little brother who stole their bats. By the end of the season, Tanvir came home talking about Madhuri's googly. His Dadi raised an eyebrow. "Bring her for chai," she said finally.

"Why do you sit with Anirban now?" asked Gargi's cousin after the school football match.
"He's on my team. He's the goalkeeper," Gargi said.
"But Dadi says his family eats different food, they have different gods. She says be careful."
Gargi shrugged. "He shares his luchi and aloo at lunch. It's nice. And his mum makes the same sweets as ours at Durga Puja."

I'm Leela, in Class 6. Before this year, I'd never talked to anyone from the Sikh families across the road. Some of the older kids said they were "different", and I kind of believed it.
Then our teacher put me in a science project group with Gurpreet. We had to build a water filter.
At first I was shy. Gurpreet was shy too. But we both got excited about the filter. We stayed after school, pouring muddy water through sand and charcoal.
Gurpreet's mother brought us parathas. My mother sent coconut burfi.
We won second prize. Now we walk home together every day. I don't even remember what I was worried about. Gurpreet is just Gurpreet.

qa.a: A water filter.

qa.q: How did Leela feel at first in the project group?
qa.a: Leela felt shy and a little uneasy, having heard older kids say the family was different.

qa.q: What made the friendship grow?
qa.a: Working together on a shared goal, staying after school and sharing food between families.

qa.q: How might Gurpreet have felt at the start of the project?
qa.a: Gurpreet was shy too, perhaps unsure how Leela would treat them.

passage:
Class teacher's note, Class 5

This term I paired Raghav with Bhupen for the kabaddi team and the class garden. Raghav's family moved here from Tamil Nadu; Bhupen is from an Assamese family. At first Raghav told me he didn't want to be with "the new boy" because "they talk strangely".
By week three, they were practising kabaddi together at lunch. By week six, Bhupen was teaching Raghav Assamese words, and Raghav was teaching him Tamil ones. Raghav said to me, "He's funny, Ma'am. And he likes curd rice like me."
I did not lecture them. Working together as equals for the team and the garden seems to have done more than any talk.

qa.q: What was Raghav teaching Bhupen?
qa.a: Raghav was teaching him Tamil words.

qa.q: How did Raghav seem to feel about Bhupen by week six?
qa.a: He seemed friendly and happy, laughing that Bhupen is funny and likes curd rice like him.

qa.q: What made the note-writer's approach work?
qa.a: Pairing them as equals on shared tasks like kabaddi and the garden, without lectures.

qa.q: How might Bhupen have felt when Raghav first didn't want to be with him?
qa.a: Bhupen might have felt left out or hurt as the new boy.

Diwali week, Thursday.
Dear diary, Miss made me and Yusuf partners for the diya-painting project. At first I was a bit scared, because Dadi always says 'their side of town is different' and I've never been to a Muslim friend's house. But Yusuf is SO funny. He paints faces on the diyas and names them. He's also scared of lizards, same as me! Today we went to his house to finish. His ammi gave us sheer khurma and asked about my rangoli. Their house had the same steel glasses as ours and cricket on TV. I don't know what was supposed to be different. Tomorrow we present. Yusuf wants our diyas to be called Ram and Rahim. I said yes.
Bhavna
